builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Efficient Quantization Training with Stochastic Rounding via Structured Subspace Randomness
summary: S3R-EC replaces per-element random thresholds in stochastic rounding for low-precision training with a single random threshold shared per token across the hidden dimension, plus an error-correction term subtracted from the activation and weight gradients, leaving the optimizer unchanged. The cost is additional implementation complexity in the quantization and gradient-correction path and reliance on a quantized INT8 training pipeline; there is no extra memory or optimizer cost. It can fail if the structured mean-error correction is implemented incorrectly (the abstract shows uncorrected threshold sharing degrades convergence), and the reported speedups are demonstrated only on TPU v5p, so gains on a single 24 GB GPU are unverified.
rationale: The method targets accelerator-specific INT8 training throughput validated on TPU v5p, whereas the reader has one 24 GB GPU and no foundation-model training budget, so the technique is relevant to track but not directly adoptable.
technique: Structured Subspace Stochastic Rounding with Error Correction (S3R-EC)

claims.statement: S3R-EC replaces per-element random thresholds in stochastic rounding for low-precision training with a single random threshold shared per token across the hidden dimension, plus an error-correction term subtracted from the activation and weight gradients, leaving the optimizer unchanged. The cost is additional implementation complexity in the quantization and gradient-correction path and reliance on a quantized INT8 training pipeline; there is no extra memory or optimizer cost. It can fail if the structured mean-error correction is implemented incorrectly (the abstract shows uncorrected threshold sharing degrades convergence), and the reported speedups are demonstrated only on TPU v5p, so gains on a single 24 GB GPU are unverified.
S3R-EC accelerates full INT8 training steps of dense LLMs on TPU v5p by 1.24x to 1.32x over BF16 and by 1.11x over independent element-wise SR, while matching its validation loss.
